heuristics.rule: Model the US→Canada comp cut explicitly in dollar terms before accepting a Canadian role
heuristics.condition: When a US-based PM is considering a Canadian opportunity
heuristics.action: Convert both offers to USD using current exchange rate and compare total comp including equity, not just base salary
heuristics.because: A CAD $150K offer vs. a USD $200K offer looks closer than it is — it's actually a ~46% total comp reduction, which is easy to underestimate when comparing raw numbers

heuristics.rule: Only accept a lateral Canadian role at a comp cut if Canadian PR is the explicit primary goal
heuristics.condition: When the Canadian role is the same seniority level as your current US role and comes with lower total comp
heuristics.action: Treat the comp reduction as the price of immigration security, not a career move
heuristics.because: A lateral move with a comp cut has no career upside to offset the financial loss unless immigration status is the actual objective

heuristics.rule: At Canadian companies without recent funding rounds, treat equity as near-zero in your compensation calculation
heuristics.condition: When evaluating an offer from a Canadian-founded startup that is not publicly traded and has not recently raised a significant round
heuristics.action: Base your financial decision on base salary and bonus only; assign minimal value to equity
heuristics.because: Non-public Canadian companies' equity is illiquid with uncertain upside — it cannot be treated as equivalent to vested RSUs at US public companies

heuristics.rule: At Amazon Canada, do not evaluate the offer on Year 1 compensation
heuristics.condition: When evaluating an Amazon Canada PM offer
heuristics.action: Model total comp across all 4 years of the RSU vesting schedule, weighting Years 3–4 heavily
heuristics.because: Amazon's compensation is front-loaded with RSUs on an uneven vesting schedule — Year 1 is the lowest total comp year and misrepresents the actual package value

heuristics.rule: To close the Canada–US comp gap without relocating, target Principal PM or Director level at a major Canadian employer
heuristics.condition: When a Canadian-based PM is evaluating whether the comp gap justifies relocating to the US
heuristics.action: Assess whether a realistic level progression to Principal or Director in Canada would close the gap relative to mid-level US roles before deciding to relocate
heuristics.because: A Principal PM or Director in Canada at a major employer can reach CAD $220,000–$280,000, which is competitive with non-FAANG mid-level US roles when quality of life and immigration security are factored in

decision_factors.factor: Title and scope jump vs. lateral move
decision_factors.why_it_matters: A significantly more senior Canadian role may justify a total comp reduction; a lateral move does not
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Compare the scope, team size, and title level of the Canadian offer against what you would realistically achieve in the US within 12–18 months

decision_factors.why_it_matters: For some candidates, Canadian permanent residency is the primary goal, which changes the entire comp calculus
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine whether the candidate is actively pursuing PR or has existing status — if PR is the goal, a comp cut is effectively the price of that security

decision_factors.why_it_matters: RSUs at US public companies are liquid from vest date; equity at Canadian private companies is illiquid and may never pay out
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify whether the company is publicly traded, recently funded, or pre-IPO — then discount equity accordingly

decision_factors.why_it_matters: US-parented companies operating in Canada (Amazon, Google, Microsoft) offer RSU compensation that meaningfully closes the Canada–US gap; Canadian-founded companies generally do not
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check whether the company is a subsidiary of a US public company or a Canadian-founded entity with or without recent funding

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Ontario marginal tax at $150K+ is 43–49%, versus typical US tech worker effective rates of 22–24% federal — this compounds the headline comp gap
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Calculate after-tax take-home on both offers, not just gross total comp

decision_factors.factor: Career stage and level progression runway
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The Canada–US comp gap narrows significantly at senior levels; the absolute gap is largest at mid-career PM roles
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Map current level to realistic next 1–2 promotions and model total comp at those levels in both markets

decision_factors.factor: Quality of life and non-financial factors
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The source explicitly frames these as legitimate offsets to the comp gap for Canadian-based PMs
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Treat as a personal weighting factor — the source does not quantify this but presents it as a real variable in the stay-vs-relocate decision

decision_factors.factor: Company funding stage for Canadian scale-ups
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Equity compensation at Canadian fintech and scale-ups varies significantly by funding stage and growth trajectory
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Review most recent funding round, revenue trajectory, and IPO likelihood before assigning any value to equity component

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a Canadian role for immigration security at a lateral level
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The comp reduction is permanent in baseline terms — future raises and equity grants are anchored to a lower starting point, compounding the gap over time
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: US-based PMs mid-career who underestimate how long they will stay in Canada and how the anchoring effect compounds

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing a Canadian bank digital division over a tech company for PM stability
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Lower RSU exposure means lower upside, but bonus structures at banks are larger — the comp mix is different, not just lower, which affects how you should negotiate and plan
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PMs who benchmark their Canadian bank offer against tech company offers without adjusting for the bonus-vs-equity composition difference

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Joining Amazon Canada for the brand name and RSUs
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Year 1 total comp is significantly lower than the offer appears due to uneven RSU vesting — cash flow in Year 1 may be insufficient if the candidate has high fixed costs
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PMs who optimize for the 4-year average comp number without stress-testing Year 1 cash flow

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Staying in Canada and targeting level progression to close the comp gap
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The path to Principal PM or Director to close the gap requires 3–6+ more years and is not guaranteed — the opportunity cost of that time versus relocating to the US is rarely modeled explicitly
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Mid-career Canadian PMs who treat level progression as a certain path rather than a probabilistic one

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Evaluating Canadian startup equity as meaningful compensation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Illiquid equity at Canadian-founded private companies has historically underdelivered relative to US counterparts — treating it as equivalent to US RSUs systematically overstates total comp
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PMs transitioning from US roles who are accustomed to liquid RSU compensation and apply the same mental model to Canadian startup equity

failure_patterns.pattern: Comparing Canadian and US offers using gross base salary only
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Base salary is the most visible number in an offer letter; equity and tax implications require active modeling that most candidates do not do
failure_patterns.consequence: Candidate accepts a Canadian offer believing the gap is small, then realizes after-tax take-home and total comp including equity is 40–50% lower than the US alternative
warning_signs: Candidate says 'the salaries are pretty close' when comparing CAD and USD figures without converting
Candidate does not ask about RSU vesting schedule or grant size during negotiation

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating Government of Canada Job Bank salary data as representative of tech PM compensation
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: It is a government authoritative source and appears credible; candidates may not realize it captures all industries and company sizes, systematically understating tech-sector pay
failure_patterns.consequence: PM undervalues their market rate, accepts below-market offers, and has a weak negotiation anchor
warning_signs: Candidate cites Job Bank median as their comp benchmark without cross-referencing Glassdoor or Robert Half tech-specific data
Candidate believes $112K national median is the ceiling for PM roles rather than a cross-industry floor

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting a US→Canada lateral move framed as a 'career opportunity' without modeling the comp reduction
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The framing of the opportunity — new city, new company, new challenge — obscures the financial reality; candidates anchor on the narrative rather than the numbers
failure_patterns.consequence: A 46% total comp reduction that was avoidable, with no career upside to compensate
warning_signs: Candidate is excited about the company or city but has not converted the offer to USD and compared it to current total comp
Candidate describes the move as 'a slight pay cut' when the actual gap is 30–50%

failure_patterns.pattern: Assuming Canadian FAANG offices (Amazon, Google, Microsoft Canada) pay the same as US headquarters
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Same brand, same manager title, same interview process — candidates assume compensation is globally standardized
failure_patterns.consequence: Candidate is surprised post-offer that Canadian FAANG total comp is significantly lower than US FAANG, and may have already declined US opportunities
warning_signs: Candidate has not looked up Canadian-specific Glassdoor data before entering the interview process
Candidate negotiates using US FAANG comp bands as leverage without verifying whether Canadian bands are equivalent

diagnostic_questions.question: Is immigration status or Canadian PR a primary goal, or is this purely a career and compensation decision?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the comp reduction of a Canadian role is acceptable as the price of a non-financial goal or whether it needs to be justified on career/financial terms alone
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Model the comp reduction explicitly as the cost of PR — is it within an acceptable range given the timeline to PR status?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The decision should be evaluated purely on total comp in USD terms and career scope — apply the lateral vs. senior-role filter

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the Canadian employer a US-parented public company, a Canadian public company, or a Canadian private company?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: How to value the equity component of the offer — liquid RSUs vs. illiquid startup equity vs. no equity
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If US-parented public: include RSU value in total comp at current market price; model vesting schedule carefully (especially for Amazon)
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If Canadian private: assign near-zero value to equity for financial planning purposes; evaluate the role on base and bonus only

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you converted both offers to USD and compared after-tax take-home, not just gross total comp?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the candidate is aware of the full magnitude of the Canada–US gap including the tax differential
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What is the USD after-tax delta, and what non-financial factors are you treating as offsets to that delta?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Do this calculation before proceeding — the gap is typically 40–50% larger than it appears when comparing gross numbers in local currencies

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the Canadian role a title and scope increase relative to your current role, or a lateral move?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether there is career upside to offset the comp reduction
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: How many years would it take to reach that level organically at your current employer, and what is the comp difference over that period?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: A lateral move to Canada with a comp cut has no career justification — the only justification is immigration or quality of life

diagnostic_questions.question: For Amazon Canada offers: have you modeled Year 1 cash flow specifically, not just the 4-year average?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the candidate understands Amazon's uneven RSU vesting and can sustain their financial obligations in Year 1
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Is Year 1 take-home sufficient for your fixed costs in the new location including Toronto or Vancouver housing costs?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Request the RSU vesting schedule breakdown by year before accepting — Year 1 is the lowest and may be significantly below the headline number

industry_realities.common_belief: Canadian FAANG offices pay comparable salaries to US offices because they're the same companies
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canadian FAANG total comp is 25–40% lower in USD terms than US equivalents at the same seniority level — the same employer operates different compensation bands by country
industry_realities.implication: Never use US FAANG comp data as a negotiation anchor for a Canadian FAANG role without first researching Canadian-specific bands on Glassdoor CA

industry_realities.common_belief: The Government of Canada Job Bank is a reliable benchmark for tech PM salaries
industry_realities.actual_reality: Job Bank data (NOC 20012 national median: $112K) captures all industries and company sizes and systematically understates tech-sector PM compensation at major employers
industry_realities.implication: Use Job Bank data only as a cross-industry floor, not a ceiling or a negotiation anchor — Senior PMs at major tech employers earn $155K–$230K CAD, well above the national median

industry_realities.common_belief: Canadian startup equity is comparable in value to RSUs at US public companies
industry_realities.actual_reality: Non-public Canadian company equity is illiquid and has historically uncertain upside; US public company RSUs are liquid from vest date and benchmarkable at current market price
industry_realities.implication: When evaluating Canadian startup offers, strip out the equity value for financial planning purposes and make your decision based on cash compensation alone

industry_realities.common_belief: The Canada–US PM salary gap is a fixed, permanent disadvantage regardless of level
industry_realities.actual_reality: The gap narrows significantly at senior levels — a Principal PM or Director in Canada at a major employer can reach CAD $220,000–$280,000, which is competitive with non-FAANG mid-level US roles
industry_realities.implication: Level progression in Canada is a legitimate strategy for closing the gap — but it must be modeled against the time cost and probability of promotion, not assumed as automatic

industry_realities.common_belief: Canadian PM compensation is primarily base salary plus a small bonus, similar to the US structure
industry_realities.actual_reality: Base salary is 80–90% of total cash comp for most Canadian roles — RSU compensation is significant only at Shopify and US-parented companies; Canadian bank digital roles have larger bonus components instead
industry_realities.implication: The comp mix matters for negotiation strategy — at a Canadian bank, negotiate the bonus structure and percentage; at Shopify or Amazon Canada, negotiate the RSU grant size and vesting terms

industry_realities.common_belief: Vancouver PM salaries are lower than Toronto because it is a smaller market
industry_realities.actual_reality: Vancouver PM salary levels are comparable to Toronto within ±5–10%, but housing costs in Vancouver are higher — making Vancouver effectively more expensive on a comp-to-cost basis despite similar nominal salaries
industry_realities.implication: When comparing Toronto vs. Vancouver offers at similar comp levels, factor in the higher Vancouver housing cost as a real reduction in effective compensation

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Compares gross base salary numbers across offers, possibly without converting currencies, and anchors on the largest headline number
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Converts all offers to the same currency, models after-tax take-home, assigns liquidity-adjusted value to equity, and compares total comp including vesting schedules year by year
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A $200K USD offer vs. CAD $150K offer looks much closer than it is — a junior framing leads to accepting a 46% effective pay cut while believing it was a minor reduction

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats all equity as equivalent — a $50K RSU grant at a Canadian private startup is mentally equivalent to a $50K RSU grant at Amazon
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Discounts illiquid private equity heavily or to zero for financial planning; assigns full value only to vested RSUs at public companies with liquid markets
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Overvaluing illiquid equity leads to accepting below-market cash compensation in exchange for an upside that may never materialize

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Cites government or national median data (e.g., Job Bank $112K national median) as the relevant benchmark for a tech PM role
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Uses role-specific, industry-specific, and city-specific data (Robert Half, Glassdoor CA, company-specific ranges) and treats national medians as a cross-industry floor only
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Using the wrong benchmark anchor results in undervaluing your market rate and entering negotiations from a position of artificial weakness

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Reasoning about the Canada–US comp decision
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Frames the decision as binary: Canada or the US, based on which total comp number is higher
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Frames the decision as multi-variable: models comp gap in USD after tax, weights immigration security as an explicit variable with a dollar value, assesses level progression probability in each market, and factors in quality-of-life offsets
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The binary framing leads to suboptimal decisions — a Canadian who could close the gap via promotion in 2 years may unnecessarily relocate; a US PM may accept a comp cut without understanding its permanence
